label: strong
answer: Demand-pull inflation is one cause of inflation in Australia. It occurs when aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's productive capacity, for example when strong household consumption and government spending outpace supply. Firms respond to the excess demand by raising prices, so the general price level rises.

label: strong
answer: When Australia's inflation rate is higher than that of its trading partners, the prices of Australian-made goods and services rise relative to foreign goods. Because input costs such as wages and materials are higher, Australian exporters must charge more in world markets, so foreign buyers switch to cheaper competitors and export volumes fall. At the same time imports become relatively cheaper than domestic substitutes, so Australians buy more imports. This loss of price competitiveness worsens the balance on goods and services and can reduce output and jobs in trade-exposed industries.

label: strong
answer:
Labour market policies affect inflation mainly through their impact on labour costs and productivity.
The Fair Work Commission's annual increase in the national minimum wage raises labour costs for firms. If wage growth exceeds productivity growth, unit labour costs rise and firms pass these costs on as higher prices, adding to cost-push inflation. Higher wages also raise disposable incomes for low-paid workers, who have a high marginal propensity to consume, which adds to demand-pull pressure. However, because only around a fifth of workers are paid award or minimum rates, the overall inflationary impact of a modest increase is limited.
Education, training and employment programs, such as fee-free TAFE places, work in the opposite direction over the longer term. By improving skills they ease labour shortages, lower the risk of wage-price pressure in tight labour markets and raise labour productivity, which reduces unit labour costs and allows the economy to grow without accelerating inflation.
Enterprise bargaining ties pay rises to productivity gains at the workplace level, which also limits cost inflation. Overall, wage-setting policies can add to inflation in the short term, while supply-side labour market policies help contain it over time, supporting the RBA's 2-3% target.

label: strong
answer:
Name: World Trade Organization (WTO).
Australia's participation in the WTO means it must apply the most-favoured-nation principle and reduce tariffs and other barriers in line with multilateral negotiations. One implication is that Australian exporters, especially agricultural producers, gain more secure access to large overseas markets because member countries are bound by agreed tariff ceilings. The WTO's dispute settlement process also allows Australia to challenge unfair trade barriers, as it did over Chinese tariffs on Australian barley in 2020-2023, which helps protect export income and employment in rural industries.

International economic integration is the process of the world's economies becoming more connected through trade, finance and technology. Several factors have contributed to this.
Firstly, trade liberalisation has reduced tariffs and quotas. Through the WTO and free trade agreements such as RCEP and AUSFTA, countries have lowered barriers, so trade in goods and services has grown faster than world output. This means countries specialise in what they are good at and sell to each other.
Secondly, improvements in technology, transport and communication have reduced the cost of doing business across borders. Container shipping, the internet and cheaper air travel mean firms can sell globally and coordinate production in many countries. Transnational corporations such as Apple use global supply chains, which increases integration.
Thirdly, financial deregulation has increased financial flows. Many countries floated their exchange rates and removed capital controls in the 1980s and 1990s, so money can move quickly between countries for investment. Foreign direct investment has grown and this links economies together.
Finally, the international division of labour and migration have contributed, as workers move to where jobs are and production is located where costs are lowest.
In conclusion, trade liberalisation, technology, financial deregulation and transnational corporations have all contributed to international economic integration.

answer:
International economic integration is the growing interdependence of national economies through flows of goods and services, capital, technology and labour. Gross world product has grown from about US$50 trillion in 2000 to over US$110 trillion today, and world trade has risen to around 60 per cent of global GDP, showing how far integration has progressed. Several interrelated factors explain this.
First, trade liberalisation has lowered the cost of exchange between countries. Average world tariffs fell from around 9 per cent in the mid-1990s to under 3 per cent today as WTO rounds and over 350 regional trade agreements, such as RCEP and the Australia-UK FTA, removed barriers. Lower protection lets countries specialise according to comparative advantage, raising the volume of trade and linking production across borders. Australia's tariff cuts from the 1980s, for example, helped lift trade from about 30 to around 45 per cent of GDP.
Second, financial deregulation and the floating of exchange rates have integrated capital markets. When Australia floated the dollar in 1983 and removed capital controls, foreign capital could flow freely. Daily foreign exchange turnover now exceeds US$7 trillion. Because capital can move instantly to the highest risk-adjusted return, interest rates, asset prices and business cycles are now synchronised, as the 2008 global financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic recession showed when shocks spread across economies within weeks.
Third, advances in transport and communication technology have reduced the costs of distance. Containerisation cut shipping costs dramatically, and the internet allows services such as finance, education and software to be traded digitally. This has allowed transnational corporations to fragment production into global value chains. Apple designs products in the United States, sources components from Korea and Japan and assembles in China and Vietnam, so trade in intermediate goods now accounts for around 70 per cent of world trade.
Fourth, the international division of labour and migration have deepened integration. Emerging economies such as China and India joined the global labour market, shifting manufacturing to lower-cost locations while advanced economies specialise in services. Migration and remittances, now over US$650 billion a year, further connect economies.
Finally, international organisations and forums including the WTO, IMF, World Bank and G20 have promoted integration by setting trade rules, providing finance and coordinating responses to crises. However, rising protectionism, such as US tariffs on China since 2018 and supply-chain reshoring after COVID-19, shows integration can slow when governments prioritise security over efficiency.
In conclusion, trade liberalisation, financial deregulation, technology, TNCs and the international division of labour have combined, supported by international institutions, to make the global economy far more integrated, even though recent protectionism has slowed the pace.
